beats.trigger: ## Multi-Agent Systems
beats.got: nothing new, it's the module title

beats.trigger: Hire three agents to search. Three more to decide.
beats.got: Agents do the searching and the deciding. As the person who owns hiring, I notice that it says 'hire'.

beats.trigger: [Schedule your personal agent](exercises/personal-agent-homework.md) to read your challenge memory for a week.
beats.got: There is homework before the day, with three links. I won't open most of them.

beats.trigger: **Evaluate** when splitting pays off, independent tasks beat forked helpers, or one agent wins
beats.got: I'll learn when to use several agents and when one is enough. 'Dialects' and 'forked helpers' are jargon I'd have to ask about.

beats.trigger: What do you expect will get lost between them?
beats.got: The question is what gets lost in handoffs. That is the same question I ask when work passes between people.

beats.trigger: Writing a file changes your folder. Sending to Slack changes another system.
beats.got: An agent that acts on other systems needs a boundary and an approval step. That is a rule I could write into a policy.

beats.trigger: Push back hard when the first answer restates the problem.
beats.got: I ask the agent for the one thing that unblocks everything else, and I keep pushing until it stops restating the problem. It's a thinking exercise, which I like. It's still a bit abstract for me.

beats.trigger: Paste each retriever prompt and confirm its short list quickly.
beats.got: Four sessions, five prompts, and a lot of pasting. I couldn't tell who does what, and nothing in it is about people.

beats.trigger: You can't yet tell if it is right; that is expected. Hold the doubt, name it, don't fix it here.
beats.got: The output may sound convincing and still be wrong, and I should say so openly. I can take that to my leadership team.

beats.trigger: Your team will ask: *when do I split, and how?*
beats.got: Now it's a lecture on when to use several agents and when to use one.

beats.trigger: Build one agent per recurring workflow: a single `.md` file, guardrailed for that job.
beats.got: The unit is the workflow, not the person or the role. That is a better way to think about role design than 'which jobs go'.

beats.trigger: If one agent can produce what you need, use one.
beats.got: Start with one agent and split only when you have a reason. Fewer moving parts also means fewer people confused.

beats.trigger: A legal-policy agent shouldn't have customer-data access.
beats.got: Split agents by who may see what: access, dialect, stance. Access is a GDPR and works-council question I will be asked.

beats.trigger: Split for a reason, not because "three is more thorough"
beats.got: More agents don't mean better work. Hype is the warning here.

beats.trigger: The stances bring the variety. The frame brings the choice.
beats.got: Without a framework the agent just averages views. A good question needs a structure to force a choice, the way a leadership meeting does.

beats.trigger: Could one prompt produce the same quality of output?
beats.got: Nothing new, it repeats the 'start with don't' point.

beats.trigger: **Helper agents in one session (the Phase 2 move).**
beats.got: There are two ways to set it up, sessions or helpers. The names are technical and I'd need someone to explain them to me.

beats.trigger: Different tools: sessions; shared tools: helper agents.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Splitting creates handoffs, and handoffs are where work goes wrong.
beats.got: Handoffs between agents fail the way handoffs between teams fail. I know that problem well from my own organisation.

beats.trigger: A whole module showed multi-agent works. Don't apply it to everything.
beats.got: The course tells me not to overuse what it just taught. I like that it undersells itself.

beats.trigger: Agents get stuck: wrong source, three views averaged into mush, the wrong file written, confident right before a failed handoff.
beats.got: Agents fail in recognisable ways, and one of them is sounding confident right before it fails.

beats.trigger: This prompt is long. Make your own variant.
beats.got: There is a long prompt for diagnosing a stuck system. I'd pass this to someone technical.

beats.trigger: move the risky step from "do" to "propose."
beats.got: Fix problems at the sources, the processing or the boundary. The 'propose, don't do' idea is the part I'd keep.

beats.trigger: then rewrites the root instructions file in place and reports what changed.
beats.got: The agent rewrites its own rules file after the session. I'm not sure who owns that file or who checks it.

beats.got: A short summary of the module. I could read it out to my HR partners.

beats.trigger: [Agent Trigger List, After Module 3]
beats.got: More reading to do before the next module.

beats.trigger: Agents add non-deterministic behaviour, prompt injection (direct, or inside retrieved text) and emergent capability you can only bound.
beats.got: Agents bring new kinds of security risk on top of the normal ones. I'd need someone to translate the terms for me.

beats.trigger: An agent that works across connected systems has access to those systems.
beats.got: The worst-case question applies to employee data in HR systems. I haven't asked the works council or the DPO yet.

beats.trigger: You're close to an agent system that cracks your crux.
beats.got: The course says I'm close to a working agent system. I don't feel that close.

take_homes: Split agents by workflow and by who may see what (access, dialect, stance), not by default. Start with one agent.
Handoffs between agents are where work goes wrong, and the review doesn't check whether the result is true. A person still does that.
Moving the risky step from 'do' to 'propose' is a usable rule, and so is asking what the worst case is with a given access. I can take both to the leadership team.

monday.move: Ask one HR business partner which of our recurring people workflows an agent could prepare while a person still approves. Ask the DPO whether employee data may go into such a tool at all.
monday.who: One HR partner and the DPO
monday.when: Monday morning, before the leadership meeting
monday.stop_condition: The DPO or the works council says no or wants a formal process first. Then I stop and follow their process.
monday.blocker: Employee data in an AI tool needs the works council and the DPO, and I haven't asked yet.

misconception.why: The module never talks about headcount or roles. The idea that one agent per workflow replaces a person doing that workflow fits my worry as much as it eases it. 'Propose, don't do' and the human checks make me think people stay in the loop for now, but the module doesn't say which roles go.

one_line: Useful for knowing when not to build more agents, and the handoff and access points matter. But it's a technical day with no word on what it means for people, so I'd send my HR partners only if someone adds that.
